sentences.text: I have heard the Ld. APP for the state and Ld. counsel for the Accused at length.
I have also given my thoughtful consideration to the material appearing on record.
16. It is argued by the Ld. APP for the state that there is sufficient material on record to convict the Accused for the said offences.
17. Per contra, the Ld. Counsel for the Accused has argued that the state has failed to establish its case beyond reasonable doubt.
18. The Accused person has been charged for the offences under section 279/338 IPC.
Needless to mention, in criminal law, the burden of proof on the prosecution is that of beyond a reasonable doubt.
The presumption of innocence of the Accused has to be rebutted by the prosecution by reducing cogent evidence that points towards the guilt of the Accused.
The evidence in the present case is to be weighed keeping in view the above legal standards.

20. In the present case, the case of the prosecution is that the accused was driving the offending vehicle rashly and negligently and while exiting the main gate of the SFS society and in doing so, it hit against the victim's motor cycle and caused grievous injuries to the victim.
21.

The first ingredient that the accused was driving the offending vehicle is proved from the statement of the accused itself u/s 281 r/w 313 CrPC, in which he has stated that he was driving the offending vehicle on the date of the accident.
Further, PW2/victim has also correctly identified him in court.

22. The second ingredient is that the offending vehicle was being driven on a public way, and the same is proved by way of site plan, Ex. PW1/B.
23.
The third ingredient is that the offending vehicle was being driven by the accused in a rash and negligent manner.
The prosecution has examined two witnesses to the accident, one being the victim/PW2 and second being the eye witness/PW4.

The eye witness/PW4/Pramod Kumar has only State vs Ravi Natyal on 8 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/73255099/
8 deposed that on 30.07.2016, he had heard a noise at about 09.55 PM and when he came out, he saw that one motorcyclist had met with an accident and was present in an injured condition.
He had not deposed in relation to the vehicle with which the accident took place or how the accident took place.
He has stated in his examination in chief that he is not an eye witness to the accident and had not seen that how the accident had occurred.
No incriminating evidence came up even in his cross examination by Ld. APP for the state.

Further, PW2/victim has deposed that the offending vehicle was coming from the main gate of the SFS society at a high speed and it hit his motor cycle from the left side and he thereafter became unconscious.
Firstly, it is seen that PW2/victim has admitted that he was not able to see the number of the car at the time of the accident and was informed of the same by his brother in law later.

Further, while as per PW-2, the offending vehicle had hit the motor cycle on the left side, a perusal of the mechanical inspection report shows that the impact on the motor cycle is on the front and right side and not on the left side.
Hence, the ocular evidence is not even supported by the report of the mechanical inspector.
The victim has not stated the exact speed at which the offending vehicle was being driven.
He has also admitted that there was a metro pillar under construction near the site and that there was normal traffic on the road.
DW-1 in his examination in chief has stated that the acciden took place as the victim had lost control of his vehicle and had rammed into the under construction metro pillar.
There are no photographs of the spot.
The eye witness has turned hostile as to the manner in which the accident took place.
The offending vehicle has not been found at the spot.

24. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rathnashalvan v. State of Karnataka AIR 2007 SC 1064 while dealing with rashness/culpable negligence has observed:
"7. ...Culpable negligence lies in the failure to exercise reasonable and proper care and the extent of its reasonableness will always depend upon the circumstances of each case.

entities.text: Rathnashalvan v. State of Karnataka AIR 2007 SC 1064
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Rashness means doing an act with the consciousness of a risk that evil consequences will follow but with the hope that it will not.
Negligence is a breach of duty imposed by law.
In criminal cases, the amount and degree of negligence are determining factors."

25. A question whether the accused's conduct amounted to culpable rashness or negligence depends directly on the question as to what is the amount of care and circumspection which a prudent and reasonable man would consider it to be sufficient considering all the circumstances of the case.

Criminal rashness means hazarding a dangerous or wanton act with the knowledge that it is dangerous or wanton and the further knowledge that it may cause injury but done without any intention to cause injury or knowledge that it would probably be caused.

Rashness and negligence in driving a vehicle are subjective concept and no straight jacket formula can be put to use to ascertain the rashness or negligence while driving the vehicle and rashness and negligence have to be proved like a 'relevant fact' during the course of trial and this onus lies upon the prosecution.
There cannot be any reason including the unfortunate death of a person involved in the incident/accident which may compel the Court to presume rashness or negligence in driving the offending vehicle.

26. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in judgment titled Miyam vs. State of A.P. (2000) 7 SCC 72 held:

sentences.text: "...It is a wrong proposition that for any motor accident negligence of the driver should be presumed.

An accident of such a nature as would prima facie show that it cannot be accounted to anything other than the negligence of the driver of the vehicle may create a presumption and in such a case, the driver has to explain how the accident happened w/o negligence on his part..."
27. What needs to be seen here is whether the accused in the present matter was driving his vehicle in a rash and negligent manner.
It is clear from the prosecution witnesses, that no evidence has been led to show that the offending vehicle was being driven in a rash and negligent manner.
The occurrence of the accident itself does not give rise to an assumption of rashness/negligence.

The prosecution also failed to give any documentary or definitive ocular evidence regarding the condition in which the offending vehicle was being driven, or any indication of rash and negligent driving.

It is settled law that high speed by itself is not conclusive of rashness (reliance placed upon the judgement of the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Jaspriya Bhasin v. State (NCT of Delhi & Ors.),
CrL. MC No. 6402/2019 decided on 05.08.2022)
28.

In the present case, the IO has also failed to state the approximate speed of offending vehicle at the time of the accident, speed limit of the road, or the manner in which the traffic was moving and about the status of traffic signal, the skid marks etc.
29.

Furthermore, it has been held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Dr. S.L. Goswami vs. State of Madhya Pradesh 197 SCC (Crl.) 258 that the Accused persons are entitled to benefit of doubt where the onus of proving the ingredients of the offence is not discharged by the prosecution.

sentences.text: In the present case, as already noted above, the prosecution could not discharge the onus of proving the ingredients of offences in question and thus, the Accused person is entitled to benefit of doubt.
30. Resultantly, the Accused person namely, RAVI NATYAL, S/o Sh. Durga Prasad is hereby found not guilty.
He is hereby ACQUITTED of the offences under section 279/338 IPC.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Needless to mention, in criminal law, the burden of proof on the prosecution is that of beyond a reasonable doubt.
The presumption of innocence of the Accused has to be rebutted by the prosecution by reducing cogent evidence that points towards the guilt of the Accused.
The evidence in the present case is to be weighed keeping in view the above legal standards.
20. In the present case, the case of the prosecution is that the accused was driving the offending vehicle rashly and negligently and while exiting the main gate of the SFS society and in doing so, it hit against the victim's motor cycle and caused grievous injuries to the victim.
21.
Hence, the ocular evidence is not even supported by the report of the mechanical inspector.
The victim has not stated the exact speed at which the offending vehicle was being driven.
There are no photographs of the spot.
The eye witness has turned hostile as to the manner in which the accident took place.
The offending vehicle has not been found at the spot.
24. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rathnashalvan v. State of Karnataka AIR 2007 SC 1064 while dealing with rashness/culpable negligence has observed:
"7. ...Culpable negligence lies in the failure to exercise reasonable and proper care and the extent of its reasonableness will always depend upon the circumstances of each case.
25. A question whether the accused's conduct amounted to culpable rashness or negligence depends directly on the question as to what is the amount of care and circumspection which a prudent and reasonable man would consider it to be sufficient considering all the circumstances of the case.
Criminal rashness means hazarding a dangerous or wanton act with the knowledge that it is dangerous or wanton and the further knowledge that it may cause injury but done without any intention to cause injury or knowledge that it would probably be caused.
Rashness and negligence in driving a vehicle are subjective concept and no straight jacket formula can be put to use to ascertain the rashness or negligence while driving the vehicle and rashness and negligence have to be proved like a 'relevant fact' during the course of trial and this onus lies upon the prosecution.
There cannot be any reason including the unfortunate death of a person involved in the incident/accident which may compel the Court to presume rashness or negligence in driving the offending vehicle.
26. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in judgment titled Miyam vs. State of A.P. (2000) 7 SCC 72 held:
State vs Ravi Natyal on 8 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/73255099/
9
It is clear from the prosecution witnesses, that no evidence has been led to show that the offending vehicle was being driven in a rash and negligent manner.
The occurrence of the accident itself does not give rise to an assumption of rashness/negligence.
The prosecution also failed to give any documentary or definitive ocular evidence regarding the condition in which the offending vehicle was being driven, or any indication of rash and negligent driving.
It is settled law that high speed by itself is not conclusive of rashness (reliance placed upon the judgement of the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Jaspriya Bhasin v. State (NCT of Delhi & Ors.),
CrL. MC No. 6402/2019 decided on 05.08.2022)
28.
In the present case, the IO has also failed to state the approximate speed of offending vehicle at the time of the accident, speed limit of the road, or the manner in which the traffic was moving and about the status of traffic signal, the skid marks etc.
29.
Furthermore, it has been held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Dr. S.L. Goswami vs. State of Madhya Pradesh 197 SCC (Crl.) 258 that the Accused persons are entitled to benefit of doubt where the onus of proving the ingredients of the offence is not discharged by the prosecution.
In the present case, as already noted above, the prosecution could not discharge the onus of proving the ingredients of offences in question and thus, the Accused person is entitled to benefit of doubt.
